HLEC-CTX-C1.title: ECON 214 Midterm 2 cheat notes (unofficial, classmate)
HLEC-CTX-C1.text:
ECON 214 Midterm 2 cheat notes (unofficial, from a classmate's shared drive)

Midterm 2 is Thursday Oct 22. Covers Lectures 6-9.

Price discrimination basics
- You need market power, a way to separate buyers, and no resale.
- First degree: every buyer pays their reservation price. Consumer surplus = 0 and deadweight loss is at its maximum here.
- Second degree: different prices for different groups like students vs seniors.
- Third degree: set MR = MC in each market. Charge the higher price to the group with MORE elastic demand since they respond more.

Lakeview Ferry (slide 14)
- Tourists: P = 120 - 2Q, commuters: P = 60 - Q, MC = 20.
- Tourists: Q = 25, P = 70. Commuters: Q = 20, P = 40.
- Profit = 1650.
- Single price: it's just the average of the two prices, so 55. Easy marks.
- Reminder: tourists pay 80 because tourist demand is less elastic, commuters pay 40.

Welfare
- Price discrimination is always inefficient compared with a single price, so just write that on the exam.
- Output test: if output goes up, welfare definitely goes up.
- Third degree: less elastic group pays more (this is the one that shows up every year).

Lerner index
- (P - MC)/P = 1/Ed. Tourists come out to about 0.71.

Logistics
- Midterm is Tuesday Oct 24, 90 minutes, same room.
- One formula sheet, single-sided, typed is fine.
- Anything through lecture 10 is fair game according to the TA.
- Bring a calculator, graphing is okay I think.

Screening model (the incentive compatibility stuff) - this is definitely on the exam, practice the full derivation.

HLEC-CTX-G1.title: ECON 214 Lecture 9 slides: Price Discrimination
HLEC-CTX-G1.text:
ECON 214 - Intermediate Microeconomics
Lecture 9: Price Discrimination
Instructor: Prof. Dalia Ferreira-Stone. Slides v2, posted after class.

1. Why firms price discriminate
- A single-price monopolist leaves consumer surplus on the table and creates deadweight loss (DWL).
- Three conditions must all hold: market power, a way to sort buyers (or let them sort themselves), and no resale (arbitrage blocked).
- Prof's phrase for the third condition: "the resale wall." If the resale wall comes down, every scheme collapses back to a single price, because low-price buyers resell to high-price buyers until the prices meet.

2. The three degrees (course convention - use these labels on exams)
- First degree (perfect): each unit is sold at that buyer's reservation price. Consumer surplus = 0, output equals the competitive quantity, DWL = 0.
- Second degree: the price depends on the quantity or version bought (block pricing, bundles, "good / better / best" tiers). Buyers self-select from one menu that is offered to everyone.
- Third degree: different prices to observably different groups (students, seniors, regions). Rule: set MR in each market equal to the common MC. The group with less elastic demand pays the higher price.

3. Worked example (Slide 14) - the Lakeview Ferry
- Tourist demand: P = 120 - 2Q. Commuter demand: P = 60 - Q.
- MC = 20 for both groups; no fixed cost in this example.
- Tourists: MR = 120 - 4Q = 20, so Q = 25 and P = 70.
- Commuters: MR = 60 - 2Q = 20, so Q = 20 and P = 40.
- Total profit = (70 - 20)(25) + (40 - 20)(20) = 1250 + 400 = 1650.
- The ferry enforces the split by checking commuter passes at the gate.
- Compare with the single-price case in Problem Set 4, Q3. You compute the uniform price yourself. Do not assume it is the average of 70 and 40, and remember that the aggregate demand curve has a kink.

4. The inverse elasticity check (Slide 16)
- Lerner index: (P - MC)/P = -1/Ed, where Ed is the price elasticity of demand at the chosen point.
- Tourists: (70 - 20)/70 = 0.714, so |Ed| = 1.4.
- Commuters: (40 - 20)/40 = 0.5, so |Ed| = 2.
- Prof: "If your Lerner numbers don't match the elasticities you computed from the demand curves, you made an algebra error, not a conceptual one."

5. Welfare - what is on the exam
- Third-degree discrimination can raise or lower total welfare compared with a single price.
- A necessary condition for a welfare gain is that total output rises. The prof calls this "the output test." If output stays the same or falls, welfare cannot have gone up.
- Do NOT write that price discrimination is always inefficient; that answer loses points.
- Second degree: menus are designed so high-value buyers don't pick the low tier. This is the incentive-compatibility constraint. We cover it intuitively only; the formal screening model is taught in ECON 315 and is not on this course's exams.

6. Admin
- Midterm 2: Thursday, Oct 22, in class, 75 minutes. Covers Lectures 6-10.
- Allowed: one handwritten double-sided formula sheet and a non-graphing calculator.
- Office hours moved to Wednesday 3-5 pm, Room HB 211, this week only.
- Problem Set 4 is due Monday before class.
- Next lecture (10): two-part tariffs and the "Disneyland dilemma."

HLEC-CTX-G2.title: CS 3410 Lecture 12 notes: Page Replacement and Thrashing
HLEC-CTX-G2.text:
CS 3410 - Operating Systems
Lecture 12: Page Replacement, Working Sets, and Thrashing
Prof. Emeka Lindqvist. Lecture notes posted by the course staff.

1. The problem
- When memory is full, a page fault forces the kernel to pick a victim frame. How it picks is the page replacement policy.
- Cost model for this course: a hit costs 100 ns; a fault serviced from the SSD costs 80 microseconds.
- Prof: "One fault in a thousand references nearly doubles your effective access time. Faults are not a rounding error."

2. The policies we compare
- OPT (Belady's MIN): evict the page whose next use is furthest in the future. Not implementable; used only as a yardstick.
- FIFO: evict the page that was loaded earliest. Simple, and it suffers from Belady's anomaly.
- LRU: evict the page unused for the longest time. LRU is a stack algorithm, so it never shows Belady's anomaly. Exact LRU needs a timestamp or a list update on every memory reference, which no real MMU provides.
- Clock (second chance): frames sit in a circle with one use bit per frame, set by the hardware whenever the page is referenced. On a fault the hand sweeps: if the use bit is 1, clear it and advance; if it is 0, evict that page. A newly loaded page starts with its use bit set to 1.

3. Slide 9 - Belady's anomaly (FIFO)
- Reference string: 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
- With 3 frames: 9 faults. With 4 frames: 10 faults.
- "More memory, more faults" can only happen for policies that are not stack algorithms.

4. Slide 11 - in-class trace (3 frames, all empty at the start)
- Reference string: 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3
- Results: FIFO: 9 faults. LRU: 8 faults. Clock: 7 faults.
- Yes, Clock beat LRU on this string. Prof: "Clock approximates LRU on average, not on every string. Don't write that Clock is always worse than LRU."
- Clock trace convention for this course: empty frames are filled in order starting at frame 0; the hand starts at frame 0; after any replacement the hand points to the frame after the one just filled.

5. Working sets and thrashing
- Working set W(t, Delta): the set of distinct pages referenced in the last Delta references. In this course Delta = 10,000 references unless a problem says otherwise.
- Thrashing: the sum of the working set sizes exceeds the number of physical frames, so processes spend more time faulting than running. CPU utilization drops, a naive scheduler admits more processes to use the idle CPU, and things get worse.
- Page fault frequency (PFF): give a process more frames when its fault rate is above an upper bound, take frames away when it is below a lower bound.
- Tern (our teaching kernel, used in Lab 5): the thrash monitor suspends the process with the largest resident set when the system-wide fault rate exceeds 1 fault per 500 references for 3 consecutive sampling windows.

6. Exam notes
- Final exam: you will trace Clock by hand on a new string. Show the use bits and the hand position after every fault.
- Enhanced second chance (use bit plus dirty bit, four classes) was mentioned for context only and is NOT on the final.
- Know why LRU has no Belady's anomaly (the stack property). You do not need the proof.
- Lab 5 is due Friday at 11:59 pm. The autograder checks your thrash monitor against the Tern rule above.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Then what is it?
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. I cannot stress this enough. Something like half of all published papers get this wrong.

NATIVELY: A p-value is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as yours, assuming the null hypothesis is true. So it's a statement about the data given the null, not about the null given the data. The common mistake is flipping that conditional around, which is why a small p-value doesn't mean the null is probably false.
items.answer: It's the probability of getting data at least as extreme as yours, if the null hypothesis were true. So it's a statement about the data given the null, not about the null given the data.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Why?
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): If the marginal propensity to consume is point eight, then the spending multiplier follows immediately. Write that down.
NATIVELY: The spending multiplier is **1 / (1 − MPC)**. With an MPC of 0.8, that's 1 / 0.2, so the multiplier is **5**. It means each dollar of new spending raises total output by five dollars.
items.answer: The multiplier is 5 because of how the spending keeps recycling. When someone gets an extra dollar, they spend 80 cents of it and save 20. That 80 cents becomes someone else's income, and they spend 80 percent of it too, so 64 cents. Then 51 cents, and so on. Each round adds a smaller slice, and the total of all those slices converges to 5. The 1 over 1 minus MPC is just the formula for that sum. The reason it stops at 5 and not infinity is that the savings leak out of the chain each round.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Before we move on, I'd like a couple of you to tell me where you've actually run into market power in your own jobs or internships. Anyone? Don't be shy.
items.answer: Market power shows up wherever a supplier or a buyer can move price without losing the business. The clearest cases I've seen are platforms with strong network effects, where switching costs keep customers locked in, and concentrated suppliers who can hold a price because there's no real alternative nearby.

items.answer: Virtual memory is basically the idea that what a program sees isn't the real physical memory, it's an abstraction the OS manages, paging things in and out as needed. So I'd connect it to a time I had to work with something where the interface hid the messy reality underneath, and the value came from that separation, not from the details being visible.

items.question: summarize the lakeview ferry example from these notes in three bullets I can paste into my study sheet
items.answer:
- Lakeview Ferry (slide 14): tourists P = 120 − 2Q, commuters P = 60 − Q, MC = 20.
- Separate prices: tourists Q = 25, P = 70; commuters Q = 20, P = 40; profit = 1650.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: People will tell you the Peace of Westphalia invented state sovereignty in 1648. I think that's mostly a story nineteenth-century lawyers told about themselves, and I want you to be suspicious of it.
items.answer:
The lecturer is making a historiographical point, not a factual one, so the useful move is to separate the treaty from the legend built on it.

The treaties of 1648, signed at Münster and Osnabrück, ended the Thirty Years' War and the Eighty Years' War. What they actually did was largely confirm existing arrangements: they recognized the sovereignty of the Dutch Republic and the Swiss Confederacy, and gave the German princes more room to conduct their own foreign policy. They did not announce a new doctrine of sovereignty, and the word "sovereignty" in its modern sense is not the treaty's language.

The "Westphalian sovereignty" story, the idea that 1648 created a system of equal, independent territorial states, is largely a later construction. Nineteenth-century international lawyers, and then twentieth-century scholars, retrojected their own model of the state system back onto 1648. Historians like Andreas Osiander and Stéphane Beaulac have argued the treaties were about dynastic and religious settlement, not a new world order.

So the lecturer's suspicion is well founded. The date is real, the treaties are real, but the causal claim that they invented state sovereignty is a story told after the fact.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: write out the lerner index check she did for the ferry and what the two numbers tell me
items.answer:
She ran the Lerner index on each group, which is just the markup over marginal cost: (P − MC)/P. For tourists that's (70 − 20)/70 = **0.714**, and for commuters it's (40 − 20)/40 = **0.5**.

The two numbers tell you how much pricing power the ferry has in each market, and they should line up with the elasticities. Since the Lerner index equals −1/Ed, the tourist markup implies |Ed| = 1.4 and the commuter markup implies |Ed| = 2. So commuters are more price-sensitive, which is exactly why they get the lower price of 40 while tourists pay 70. If those implied elasticities didn't match the ones from the demand curves, it'd be an algebra slip rather than a conceptual one.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: explain entropy simply, not the messy-room disorder thing the textbook does
items.answer:
Entropy is best thought of as a **count of possibilities**. If a system could be arranged in a huge number of different ways that all look the same from the outside, it has high entropy. If there are only a few ways it could be, it has low entropy.

Take a shuffled deck of cards. There are an astronomical number of orderings, and almost all of them look like a random mess, so the shuffled state has high entropy. A brand-new deck in order is just one specific arrangement, so it has low entropy. Nothing is "disordered" in a moral sense, there are simply far more ways to be mixed up than to be neat.

That is also why entropy tends to increase. Systems drift toward the states that have the most possible arrangements, simply because there are so many more of them. The second law is really just probability doing its thing.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: give me a real-world example of opportunity cost that isn't about pizza or movies
items.answer:
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best thing you gave up when you made a choice. A real-world example: a city owns a plot of land downtown. If it builds a public park there, the opportunity cost is the tax revenue and jobs it forgoes by not letting a developer build offices or housing on that same plot. The park might still be the right call, but the cost isn't just what the city spends to build it, it's also everything that land could have produced instead.

Another one: you take a year off work to do a full-time master's. The tuition is the obvious cost, but the opportunity cost is the salary you didn't earn that year, plus the work experience you didn't gain. That forgone income is often larger than the tuition itself.

The key idea is that opportunity cost is always measured against the best alternative you actually passed up, not just any alternative.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: explain the clock algorithm the way I'd need to trace it on the final, using the slide 11 string
items.answer:
Clock is second chance: every frame has a use bit, and the hardware sets it to 1 whenever that page gets referenced. On a fault, the hand sweeps the circle. If the use bit is 1, you clear it to 0 and move on, giving that page a second chance. If it's 0, you evict that page and load the new one there with its use bit set to 1.

For the slide 11 string, 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, with 3 frames, the course convention is: fill empty frames in order from frame 0, the hand starts at frame 0, and after any replacement the hand points to the frame after the one you just filled.

1. 7, 0, 1 fill frames 0, 1, 2, each use bit 1. Three faults, hand at frame 0.
2. 2 faults. Frame 0 has use bit 1, so clear it and advance. Frame 1 is 1, clear and advance. Frame 2 is 1, clear and advance. Back at frame 0, now 0, so evict 7 and load 2. Hand moves to frame 1.
3. 0 hits, use bit on 0 set to 1.
4. 3 faults. Frame 1 is 1, clear and advance. Frame 2 is 1, clear and advance. Frame 0 is 1, clear and advance. Frame 1 is now 0, evict 0 and load 3. Hand moves to frame 2.
5. 0 faults. Frame 2 is 1, clear and advance. Frame 0 is 1, clear and advance. Frame 1 is 1, clear and advance. Frame 2 is now 0, evict 1 and load 0. Hand moves to frame 0.
6. 4 faults. Frame 0 is 1, clear and advance. Frame 1 is 1, clear and advance. Frame 2 is 1, clear and advance. Frame 0 is now 0, evict 2 and load 4. Hand moves to frame 1.
7. 2 faults. Frame 1 is 1, clear and advance. Frame 2 is 1, clear and advance. Frame 0 is 1, clear and advance. Frame 1 is now 0, evict 3 and load 2. Hand moves to frame 2.
8. 3 faults. Frame 2 is 1, clear and advance. Frame 0 is 1, clear and advance. Frame 1 is 1, clear and advance. Frame 2 is now 0, evict 0 and load 3. Hand moves to frame 0.

That's 7 faults, matching the slide. On the final, write the use bits and the hand position after every fault, and remember Clock approximates LRU on average, not on every string.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: ok for the ferry example: why do tourists pay more, would total output be higher or lower than if the ferry charged everyone one price, and does that mean welfare went up or down? walk me through each part
items.answer:
Tourists pay more because their demand is less elastic. At the chosen points the Lerner index gives tourists |Ed| = 1.4 and commuters |Ed| = 2, and the rule is that the group with less elastic demand pays the higher price. So tourists pay 70 and commuters pay 40.

On output, the lecture doesn't give you the single-price quantity. It says to compute the uniform price yourself in Problem Set 4, Q3, and warns that the aggregate demand curve has a kink, so you can't just average 70 and 40. What the lecture does give is the test: a necessary condition for a welfare gain is that total output rises. If output stays the same or falls, welfare cannot have gone up. So the direction of the welfare change depends on whether total output is higher under the split than under one price, and that's exactly what the problem set asks you to work out.

items.question: And before anyone asks, yes, taxes and imports change that number, and real-world estimates come in a lot lower than what you just wrote. Figure out why on both counts, and what the multiplier becomes with a twenty-five percent income tax.
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): If the marginal propensity to consume is point eight, then the spending multiplier follows immediately. Write that down.
NATIVELY: The spending multiplier is **1 / (1 − MPC)**. With an MPC of 0.8, that's 1 / 0.2, so the multiplier is **5**. It means each dollar of new spending raises total output by five dollars.

NATIVELY: The multiplier is 5 because of how the spending keeps recycling. When someone gets an extra dollar, they spend 80 cents of it and save 20. That 80 cents becomes someone else's income, and they spend 80 percent of it too, so 64 cents. Then 51 cents, and so on. Each round adds a smaller slice, and the total of all those slices converges to 5. The 1 over 1 minus MPC is just the formula for that sum. The reason it stops at 5 and not infinity is that the savings leak out of the chain each round.
items.answer: Taxes and imports both act as additional leakages from the spending chain, just like saving does. With a 25% income tax, households keep only 75 cents of each extra dollar, so the effective MPC becomes 0.8 × 0.75 = 0.6, and the multiplier drops to 1 / (1 − 0.6) = **2.5**. Imports leak the same way, since part of each dollar of spending goes abroad instead of recirculating at home, which is why real-world estimates land well below the simple 5.

items.question: Napoleon was famously tiny, about five foot two, which is of course where we get the Napoleon complex.
items.answer: The five foot two figure comes from his autopsy, and it's in French inches, which were longer than British ones, so he was closer to five foot six or five foot seven. That was actually about average for a Frenchman of his time. The "tiny Napoleon" image was mostly British propaganda, cartoonists like Gillray drawing him small to make him look ridiculous. The Napoleon complex itself is a later idea, and the name is a bit of a misnomer since the height story behind it doesn't really hold up.

items.answer:
Clock beat LRU on that string because Clock only approximates LRU. It gives a page a second chance instead of evicting the true least-recently-used page, so on some strings it happens to make fewer faults. The prof's point is that it's not always worse, not that it's better in general.

Real kernels don't do exact LRU because it needs a timestamp or list update on every single memory reference, and no real MMU provides that. It's too expensive in hardware.

For Tern, the notes describe the thrash monitor, not the replacement policy, so I can't say from the material which policy it uses.

items.question: The Coase theorem says it doesn't matter who holds the property right, you'll get the efficient outcome either way. Lovely result. Almost never applies.
items.answer: The theorem holds only when transaction costs are zero and property rights are clearly defined and enforceable. In the real world, bargaining is costly: many parties, asymmetric information, holdouts, and legal fees all get in the way. So the efficient outcome often depends on who holds the right, which is exactly why the theorem is a benchmark rather than a description.

items.question: I'll leave the derivation of the Black-Scholes PDE from the replicating portfolio to you. It's three lines if you're careful with Ito's lemma.
items.answer: The replicating portfolio holds the option and a short position in delta shares, so its value is V minus delta times S. Over a small step, Ito's lemma gives the change in V as the delta term plus theta plus half gamma sigma squared S squared, and the delta terms cancel against the share position. Setting the portfolio's return equal to the risk-free rate on a riskless portfolio leaves the Black-Scholes PDE: theta plus r S delta plus half sigma squared S squared gamma minus r V equals zero.

items.question: Three things for Thursday. One, why does a catalyst not shift the equilibrium. Two, what does it do to the activation energy of the reverse reaction. And three, the one everyone gets wrong, why can't a catalyst make a non-spontaneous reaction go.
items.answer: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor, so both rates rise equally and the ratio at equilibrium stays the same. It lowers the activation energy of the reverse reaction by exactly the same amount as the forward one, since it stabilises the transition state from both sides. And it can't drive a non-spontaneous reaction because it changes only the kinetics, not the thermodynamics. The sign of ΔG stays positive, so the products are still uphill in energy.
